Hi

Now I am comparing irace against my online parameter control approach.

The question is: 
If I use 600000 evaluations in my online approach, would be enough use 2000 experiments of 300 evaluations in irace (totalizing 600000 evaluations)?

messages.author: 854a0709976c2a48
messages.subject: Re: Comparing irace to online parameter control
parts:
On Monday, 6 March 2017 15:31:56 UTC, Vinicius Renan Carvalho wrote:

Hi

Now I am comparing irace against my online parameter control approach.

The question is: 
If I use 600000 evaluations in my online approach, would be enough use 2000 experiments of 300 evaluations in irace (totalizing 600000 evaluations)?

It depends what you are comparing for, but in general it doesn't make sense. If one run of the algorithm when deployed performs 600K FEs, then one run of the algorithm when training should perform 600K FEs. Parameter settings that are good for 300 FEs are not necessarily good for 600K FEs, so it doesn't make sense to train for 300 but then run with 600K (unless you do some prediction of parameter values for longer FE budget but irace doesn't do that yet).

The time required by irace (or any offline method) should not be comparable to the time required by an online method, precisely because one is offline and the other is online. Depending how you set up the experiments you will be forcing the online method to behave as an offline one or (as it seems to be your case) forcing the offline method to behave as an online one, which is obviously not going to work.

Roughly speaking, I see two ways to evaluate an online method:

* There is no time for offline training or the instances solved in practice are too heterogeneous: These two scenarios are actually the same in terms of what one would do in practice: Use a "good enough" algorithm even if it was designed (or tuned) for a slightly different problem. That is, train with a sufficiently large budget either on a heterogeneous set of similar but not exactly equal problems (or use two different but related problems, one will become the training problem and the other the testing problem, even better if you can measure and/or control the dissimilarity) to get an overall good configuration. Then compare this configuration with what the online method can achieve. One can study how many extra evaluations are required by the online method to surpass the good enough configuration. If the benchmark allows it, one can also study the trade-off between instances more distant from the training set and the performance of the online method relative to the good enough configuration. This way one can find the point at which the online method is so good and the instances so heterogeneous, that it is not worth it to train offline. Even in this case, one should tune any numerical parameters of the online method by using the same training protocol as irace is using for training the algorithm itself, since the defaults of the online method should not be set according to the "unknown and no time for offline training" instances that the online method aims to tackle. In other words, the claim is that there is no time for offline training, but you had time to design a whole online method in the meantime.

* The online method is capable of adapting dynamically various parameters that need to be adjusted throughout the run to maximise performance. In this case, one would find (or approximate, for example, by using irace) the per-instance ideal configuration and the per-training-set ideal configuration (good overall) by using enough experiments, then see how well the online method does between these two ideals. Again one can do experiments like above to see how much extra effort it requires to match either ideal. If the online method improves over the per-instance ideal (of course, the interesting question is how much extra effort and how much heterogeneity between training and testing is required to reach that situation), this is evidence that the dynamic adaptation is necessary and something that cannot be achieved offline (although one could still argue that the parameters of the online model should be tuned offline over the whole training set to prevent biases when tuning them by hand.)

In any case, it doesn't make sense to artificially reduce the evaluation budget of a single run or the number of experiments when training just to make the overall computation effort comparable. They are different scenarios that assume that different budgets are available.

(A similar situation arises when evaluating surrogate-model-based methods, such as EGO. It wouldn't make sense to run for 600K FEs EGO and compare it with a non-model-based method doing 600K as well. EGO was designed for expensive problems: If you can perform 600K evaluations, it is not an expensive problem.)

Cheers,

Manuel.
